turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: A slight tremor passed through Bimala’s hands as she reached for her needlework, the colors blurring momentarily. It seemed a precarious thing, this talk of fear and threats; surely, there were more… agreeable subjects for discussion, though she did not voice the thought.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: The implications of Sandip’s question were transparent, and he considered a direct response unnecessary. He observed that the nature of his apprehension was immaterial; what mattered was the demonstrable harm being inflicted upon those under his protection. It was, he stated, a matter for his immediate attention, and he would not indulge further speculation.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: The tremor in her hands deepened, and a delicate flush rose on her cheeks as she regarded the two men, a silent plea in her eyes that this unsettling conversation might somehow…resolve itself. It was difficult to imagine what protection could truly mean, beyond the comfortable routines of the household, and a question lingered unspoken, a quiet inquiry into the very foundations of their security.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: A theatrical sigh escaped Sandip's lips, a performance for Bimala’s benefit, naturally. One might inquire, he suggested, with a languid wave of a hand, whether demonstrable harm wasn't often, and conveniently, a matter of perspective – a canvas upon which anxieties, perhaps even… ambitions, are readily painted. Surely, even the most benevolent protector could find himself accused of oppression, depending on the artistry of the accuser.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Such artistry, it seemed, was becoming increasingly prevalent. He observed that the perception of oppression was less a matter of demonstrable fact and more a reflection of the observer's own discontent, a phenomenon easily recognized and, when necessary, addressed with appropriate measures.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: He allowed a beat, a dramatic pause, as if savoring the subtle shift in Bimala’s expression—a fleeting vulnerability, perhaps?—before adding, with a disarming smile, that it was, of course, exceedingly tiresome to be perpetually lecturing those less…enlightened on the nuances of perception. Still, one felt a certain responsibility, did one not, to illuminate the shadows, lest they fester and breed…misunderstandings. Especially when those misunderstandings threatened to obscure the very foundations of order.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: A slight inclination of the head, a gesture almost imperceptible, indicated a desire to steer the conversation elsewhere. It seemed, he thought, that shadows were not always born of discontent, but sometimes…simply existed, and it was perhaps unwise to assume malice where only darkness resided. Surely, even illumination could cast its own, unintended shadows.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: He chuckled, a low, resonant sound designed to reverberate just enough to reach Bimala’s ears, and remarked that, of course, shadows, like all things, possessed a certain…trajectory. One might, with sufficient diligence, trace their origins, wouldn't one agree, and discover that even the most seemingly benign darkness could be traced back to a source of considerable…influence. An influence, perhaps, that extended beyond the comfortable confines of this very household.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: A quiet observation escaped her lips, almost a murmur, directed towards the space between them. It seemed that tracing origins could be a perilous undertaking, particularly when one lacked a complete understanding of the landscape from which those origins sprung; a cartographer, after all, needed more than just a pencil to chart the unknown.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: The pursuit of origins, it seemed, often served as a convenient distraction from present realities. He found it prudent to focus attention on the immediate concerns of the household and its dependents, rather than chasing shadows across an increasingly turbulent landscape.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: A landscape, it occurred to her, could also be deceptive; what appeared stable and charted might shift beneath one’s feet, revealing unexpected precipices. It was not merely the cartographer's skill that was required, but also a certain… humility, a recognition that even the most detailed map was but a representation, not the territory itself.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: He allowed a theatrical sigh to escape his lips, a performance for Bimala’s benefit, naturally. Surely, Nikhil wasn't suggesting that one should simply ignore the whispers carried on the wind, the murmurs of discontent rising from beyond these manicured lawns? It was, after all, a leader’s duty to anticipate the tremors before they became an earthquake, wouldn't one agree?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: The anticipation of tremors, while perhaps admirable in some, often serves to amplify anxieties rather than mitigate them. One must distinguish between genuine threat and the manufactured anxieties of those who thrive on discord, Sandip.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: It seemed a curious thing, this insistence on dismissing anxieties as manufactured; perhaps those who felt the tremors most keenly were simply less inclined to dismiss them so readily. A leader, after all, was meant to listen as much as to anticipate, was he not?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: It is a simple matter, Sandip, to diagnose anxieties. The more difficult task lies in discerning the source of those anxieties – whether they originate from legitimate concerns or from a deliberate attempt to sow division. He finds it unproductive to engage in theatrical pronouncements about impending earthquakes when a more considered assessment of the situation is required.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip regarded Nikhil with a wry smile. A considered assessment, he remarked, was it? How delightfully quaint. One might almost imagine he was attempting to mimic the impartiality of a magistrate, Sandip continued, dispensing justice with a detachment entirely unbecoming of a landowner concerned with the stability of his holdings – and the loyalty of those who toil upon them.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: A magistrate, was he? It seemed an apt comparison, though perhaps a little harsh, Sandip. Still, one did wonder if a detachment, even a carefully cultivated one, might not also serve to…distance oneself from the realities felt so keenly by others.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Such comparisons are, he observed, readily deployed when a substantive argument is lacking. It is not detachment that guides his actions, Sandip, but a desire to maintain order and fairness, principles which, it appears, are conveniently forgotten when it suits one’s purposes.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Order and fairness, he says. How predictable. One wonders, doesn't one, if the pursuit of such lofty ideals doesn’t occasionally blind one to the…*practicalities*…of governance? After all, even the most meticulously constructed edifice requires more than just a foundation of principles to withstand the tremors of discontent.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: A tremor, was it? He wondered if it was truly a tremor, or something… else. Perhaps it was simply the sound of things shifting, and one could not always be certain of the nature of the forces at play, could one?

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip inquired of Bimala as to where she intended to flee, addressing her as Queen.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip remarked to Nikhil that he questioned why Browning was not among his books, recalling a conversation with Bimala about a college contest involving Browning's translation, and asking if Nikhil remembered it.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip explained to Nikhil that he had managed to translate Browning into Bengali, though the result was far from a lasting joy for Bengal, and that he once believed himself on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence had intervened. He then recalled old Dakshina, suggesting that had he not become a Salt Inspector, he would have been a poet.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip informed Bimala that it was pointless for her to search the bookshelves, as Nikhil had ceased reading poetry since his marriage, and that he suspected a return of his poetic inspiration.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip stated that Nikhil had come to give him a warning.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip inquired of Nikhil whether the warning concerned his poetic inspiration.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that Mahomedan preachers had been stirring up the local Mussulmans, who were agitated and might attack him at any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had come to advise flight.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil clarified to Sandip that he had come to provide information, not to offer advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip commented to Nikhil that a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for him, had the estates been his, and suggested that Nikhil's weakness was also undermining neighboring zamindars.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil pointed out to Sandip that he had not offered advice, and requested that Sandip refrain from giving it, adding that it was futile. He then stated that he needed to inform Sandip that his followers had been secretly oppressing his tenantry, and demanded that he leave his territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip questioned Nikhil, asking whether the threat was due to fear of the Mussulmans or some other apprehension.
